result:
There is something quietly astonishing about ordinary mornings. Not the dramatic kind, with thunder or revelation, but the ones that arrive in soft, practical pieces: a kettle beginning to hum, a window letting in a cautious stripe of light, a chair waiting exactly where it was left the night before. These small things do not announce themselves as important, yet they hold up whole lives.

I think people underestimate how much meaning is carried by repetition. The recurring walk to the corner store, the familiar shape of a mug in the hand, the same song played too many times and somehow not enough. Repetition can feel like a cage when we are tired of our own days, but it can also be a kind of architecture. It builds rooms in memory. It tells the body, you are here, you have been here, you will return.

A tree understands this better than we do. It does not ask each spring whether blooming is worth the effort. It does not negotiate with the rain or apologize for losing leaves in the autumn. It simply continues, which may be the most graceful form of courage. Humans are allowed to be less graceful, of course. We hesitate, revise, break, begin again. That may be our version of flowering.

And perhaps that is enough: to make a life from repetitions, interruptions, recoveries, and a few shining moments that seem, at the time, too small to matter. Later, they are the moments we keep.
